summary.text: 生 depicts a sprout rising from the ground. Early inscriptions use it for childbirth and living things, among other senses, but do not establish which use came first or that every later meaning developed from the picture.

formation.text: A semantic compound whose parts make a picture: 屮 depicts the sprout and 一 the ground beneath it. Neither part is analyzed as a sound cue. The lower stroke later changed graphically, eventually resembling 土.

components.text: 屮 is pictured as a sprout rising above the ground. It contributes to the plant image; no phonetic role is proposed.

一 is the ground line beneath the sprout in the early graphic analysis. A later mark was added beneath 屮 and developed into a horizontal stroke, changing the lower part until it resembled 土; 土 is not identified as the original component.

history.text: The selected oracle-bone-style and bronze-style forms illustrate the sprout-over-ground design. The graphic account describes early bronze forms as retaining this structure and a later mark beneath the sprout developing into a horizontal stroke. The images are modern vector renderings; the account does not provide a dated sequence of individual artifacts.
A historical dictionary describes plants emerging above soil and glosses 生 as “advance”; the graphic account treats “advance” as an extended sense, rather than the image’s core meaning.

生 was also used for 姓, “surname”: this is treated as reuse of the whole graph to write a different word, proposed because the words sounded alike or similarly. One oracle-bone phrase is read 多生, though 多甥 is an alternative. Modern Mandarin readings are shēng and xìng, and the supplied Middle Chinese forms are sraeng and sjengH; these comparisons do not prove the ancient sound match or borrowing.

uncertainties.text: The oracle-bone phrase 生月 has been read as “following month,” but “this month” and other readings have also been proposed. Its meaning and any relation to life or growth remain unsettled.

Early reported uses include childbirth, live or fresh animals, and 生月; other examples include living, lifespan, and producing or occurring. The examples do not date every use or establish an ordered development among these senses.
A conservative form 𤯓 and comparisons with other graphs are mentioned, but their chronology, ancestry, and any corruption history are not established here.

senses.text: 生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this does not establish childbirth as the character’s first meaning.
生 is reported as an adjective describing live animals in oracle-bone inscriptions. This does not establish its priority relative to the childbirth use.
One interpretation reads 生月 as “following month,” but other readings are contested. This phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.
生 is reported as an adjective for fresh or live animals; separate historical phonology entries record “fresh, raw.” No chronology connecting this sense to the others is established.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported with the sense “occur” or “produce.” The evidence does not show when or how this use developed from other senses.
A bronze-inscription example is reported with the sense “lifespan.” No transition from the other attested senses is established.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The evidence does not date this sense or show its development.

senses.period: Warring States manuscripts and later usage
senses.text: A Warring States manuscript uses 生 for living in opposition to dying. Later lexicographic evidence also records life and living, without establishing a complete development from earlier uses.

limitations.text: The inscription examples support several uses but do not establish priority or a securely dated chain among birth, living, freshness, production, lifespan, advance, and life.
The proposed sprout-and-ground image does not by itself show that every recorded word meaning developed from plant growth.
The “following month” reading of 生月 is disputed and does not demonstrate a semantic transition from growth or life to month terminology.

items.period: Shang oracle-bone script style; linked specimen 甲2402 合1977 (no artifact date assigned here)
items.caption: This Shang oracle-script form is drawn as an upright sprout rising from a short ground line, matching the interpretation of 生 as a plant emerging from soil.
items.alt: Black glyph with a central upright stalk and two angled shoots above a long horizontal ground line.
items.selection_reason: The visible sprout and ground line make the character’s proposed graphic origin especially clear.
items.rights: Commons description labels the representation public domain and identifies the Sinica source image as CC0 1.0.

items.period: Western Zhou bronze style; description links 七年趞曹鼎 and calls it mid Western Zhou
items.caption: This Western Zhou bronze-script form retains an upright, branching plant shape above a base. The lower stroke has become more substantial, consistent with the account that it developed from a mark beneath the sprout.
items.alt: Black glyph with an upright central stalk, three upper branches, and a broad irregular base.
items.selection_reason: It helps show the sprout-over-ground interpretation in a bronze-script rendering and illustrates the reported change in the lower part of the graph.
items.rights: Commons description states that the Sinica source picture is CC0 1.0; Commons labels the vector representation public domain.

limitations.text: These forms support a graphic reading of a sprout above ground, but they do not establish a dated sequence of individual artifacts or prove that every attested meaning of 生 developed from that image.
The seal-script illustration is a modern reconstruction, and the cited account does not supply a specific specimen date; it adds less than the two selected forms for explaining the graph’s origin.
